doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Gut strings and no amp
summary: Caine explains why he plays gut strings without an amp and blames amplification for louder drumming; Rowe agrees.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: I think Evan mentioned that, Evan Christopher, that you don’t play with an amp.
Okay, so tell me about that.

I mean I’m one of the few guys, there’s some other guys, but I don’t play with an amp, and I play with gut strings. And I do it, well first of all gut strings are really expensive and they go out of tune and they’re a pain in the ass. But you know all my favorite bass players, and all everybody else’s favorite bass players for the most part played like that. I mean Paul Chambers, Ray Brown back in the day, Milt Hinton, Israel Crosby, Garrison. And look man, I get it. The bass is hard to play and it’s quiet. You know? So when steel strings and amps came along it’s easier. But it fucking ruined jazz — I won’t say it ruined it, you know it allowed for the drummer to play super loud, everyone just turned shit up. Bassists sound electronic with that — you know I just don’t like it. I don’t like it. And it irks me because people say I’m like some kind of purist or whatever. It’s not that. I just think it’s much prettier and it allows the drummer to play quiet. And it reminds everyone shut the fuck up please. You can still be loud, but let’s keep everything, start here. And I’ll get off my soapbox with this last point, what other instrument but maybe the guitar has had an electronic mic added to it in the middle of the history of jazz? Like okay trumpet players, let’s just put a pick-up in your trumpet. What would they say? They’d be like hell no. Sax players, they’d be like hell no. I mean you could make it a thing about a guitar maybe you could make that argument, but it doesn’t make any sense. In the late 60s all of a sudden they changed the way the bass sounded, which changed the way everything happens.
So I don’t get it. And I’m not saying you know look, I like fusion and all that stuff. But it’s a bunch of bullshit in my opinion. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

I’m pausing because I think the bass is the most important instrument, and what you’re saying makes a lot of sense to me. If you listen to, even in pop music, if you compare how the voice was balanced with the bass back then you could hear the singer. And then you move ahead forty years and all of a sudden the bass is like all of a sudden dominating. Anyway, I think I get what you’re saying.

Yeah. And it’s like, and look, it’s hard for me — like I don’t mind not being heard on the loudest, most exciting moments of a song, as a bass player. I’m okay with that. But it just — you know there should be some variance and subtlety. And bass players don’t like to admit it either. I’ve been on the Facebook and these group chats about amps and pick- ups, and it’s always like me and two other guys who are like forget a pick-up. But nobody wants to admit — I’m telling you it’s just much easier. It’s easier to get around. To lower the string you just turn it up. You can play faster, it’s easier. It’s way harder to get a sound out of the bass, but you know, I’m in the minority, we’re in the minority in that respect.
